analysis.one_liner: Lets consumers opt out of data sharing with one click and holds executives accountable for privacy reporting.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: Senator Wyden introduced it with no cosponsors, and it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required large companies that collect people's personal information to protect it, assess their high-risk systems (including AI-driven ones), and file yearly reports certified by their top executives. Consumers could opt out of having their data shared with third parties through a government 'Do Not Track' website, get free access to what companies store about them, and challenge inaccurate records. Companies that violate the rules would face fines of up to 4 percent of annual revenue, and executives who falsely certify compliance would face criminal penalties.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers whose personal information is collected, sold, and used by large companies and data brokers. They would gain a working opt-out from data sharing, free yearly access to their stored data, the ability to challenge inaccurate information, and stronger enforcement against companies that misuse their data.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers whose data is collected and sold

how_it_helps.text: Consumers could opt out of data sharing with one click through an FTC-run 'Do Not Track' website, and covered companies would be bound by that choice — immediately for new customers, within 30 days for existing ones.

Companies with more than $50 million in revenue that hold data on over a million consumers would have to run reasonable security and privacy programs, conduct impact assessments of high-risk and AI-driven systems, and let consumers review, correct, and see who their data was shared with — free, once a year, on request.

Large companies would file annual data protection reports certified by their CEO and chief privacy officer; an executive who knowingly files a false report could face up to 20 years in prison, a fine tied to their pay, and an excise tax on their compensation.

Civil penalties for unfair trade practices would rise to the greater of $50,000 per violation or 4 percent of the company's total annual gross revenue, replacing the current $10,000-per-violation cap.

The FTC would gain a new Bureau of Technology, over 100 additional consumer-protection and enforcement staff, standardized complaint tracking for consumers, and state attorneys general could sue violators on behalf of residents.
The bill would not preempt state laws, so stronger state privacy protections would remain in place.

analysis.who_pays: Large companies that live off consumer data — tech platforms, digital advertisers, and data brokers — would bear the compliance costs, assessment requirements, and much larger fines. Some of those costs would likely reach consumers through prices, and companies could charge a fee to consumers who want a service without consenting to data sharing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tech firms, adtech, and data brokers

drawbacks.text: Companies could condition a product or service on a consumer consenting to data sharing, unless the consumer is offered the option to pay a fee for a substantially similar service — creating a pay-for-privacy tier that hits lower-income people hardest, though the bill caps the fee and exempts low-income consumers.
The impact assessments of high-risk and AI systems would be optional for companies to publish, so much of the required scrutiny could remain hidden from the public.
Companies with over $50 million in revenue would face significant compliance and assessment costs, which they could pass along to consumers in prices.

Criminal penalties of up to 20 years for executives who mis-certify reports, while aiming at accountability, could make companies cautious to the point of delay in how they report and disclose problems.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a real, enforceable opt-out from data sharing and personal accountability for executives who lie about privacy compliance — is substantial for consumers in an economy where personal data is constantly collected and traded. The costs are real but narrower: compliance burdens on data-heavy companies, possible price pass-throughs, and a pay-for-privacy option that could split consumers into tiers. The bill's biggest design weakness is that companies could keep their AI-system assessments private, limiting public scrutiny even where the law applies.

outcome.mechanism: Wyden introduced the bill in the Senate, it was referred to the Finance Committee, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended — with not a single cosponsor from either party.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden introduced the Mind Your Own Business Act on October 17, 2019; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No cosponsors ever joined the bill — the cosponsors list shows zero from either party.
No further action was ever taken: no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote appears in the action history, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, digital advertisers, and large tech platforms are better off: they continue collecting, trading, and using consumers' personal information with no federal opt-out, no executive certification requirement, and no increase in civil penalties. Consumers gain nothing from the bill's death, and the FTC gains none of the new enforcement staff it would have received.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and large tech platforms

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Technology, advertising, and data broker industry
against.role: Companies that profit from collecting and trading consumer data
against.what_they_did: Opposed comprehensive federal privacy legislation of this kind, which would have imposed compliance costs, revenue-based fines, and executive criminal liability on data-heavy firms.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls ever occurred; the bill's only sponsor was a Democrat, it drew zero cosponsors from either party, and it died in a Republican-chaired committee without any vote to measure.

industries.note: The bill squarely covered data brokers — companies that collect and sell information about people who are not their customers — and would have required them to honor opt-outs, run impact assessments, and answer to consumers directly. Their business model of trading personal information would have been constrained by law.

industries.industry: Large tech platforms and digital advertisers
industries.note: Companies over $50 million in revenue holding data on more than a million consumers would face security mandates, assessments of high-risk and AI systems, annual certified reports, and fines up to 4 percent of total annual revenue. Their revenue depends on collecting and monetizing consumer data, which the opt-out and sharing restrictions would curtail.

The FTC would have gained a Bureau of Technology, 125 additional consumer-protection and enforcement staff, new rulemaking authority, and state attorneys general as enforcement partners, letting it police data practices it currently handles with far smaller penalties.
